opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a few things, and the first one is just how fast the field is moving. Every few weeks there's a new model, open or closed, that's better at something: reasoning, coding, long context, function calling, or it's simply cheaper and faster for the same quality. If you're building a product, you don't want to wake up one morning and realize you've hard-wired yourself to something that's no longer the best option. Being model agnostic gives developers the freedom to swap in whatever works best for their use case at that moment.

The second piece is that there's no single model that wins everywhere. What we see with the developers we work with is that a real production application is rarely one model. It's more like a compound AI system. You might have a small, fast model handling classification or routing, a larger model doing the heavy reasoning, something specialized for retrieval or embeddings, maybe a vision or audio model in the pipeline. Each part has a different quality, latency, and cost profile, so you want to pick the right tool for each step instead of forcing one model to do everything.

Third, there's control and ownership. A lot of companies start by prototyping on a big proprietary API because it's the easiest way to get going. But once they move to production, they start caring about cost at scale, latency, data privacy, and being able to customize the model on their own data. Fine-tuning an open model on your proprietary data can get you quality that matches or beats a general-purpose frontier model for your specific task, at a fraction of the cost. You can only take advantage of that if your stack isn't locked into a single provider.

And finally, there's risk management. If your whole business depends on one vendor's API, you're exposed to their pricing changes, their rate limits, outages, deprecations, even shifts in model behavior between versions that you didn't ask for. Developers have been through this before with cloud infrastructure, and they've learned that keeping optionality is really valuable.

So for us, the goal is to make that optionality easy: give developers one place where they can access, evaluate, customize, and serve many different models with production-grade performance, so they can focus on building their product rather than re-architecting every time the model landscape shifts.

r001.rationale: The response says models improve rapidly and developers do not want to be hard-wired to one that may stop being the best option, so model agnosticism lets them switch.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think it comes down to a few things, and they're all rooted in how fast this space is moving.

The first is that the model landscape changes almost weekly. Six months ago the best open model for a given task might have been one thing, and today it's something completely different, and in another six months it'll be different again. If you've hard-wired your product to one model, one API, one prompt format, every one of those shifts becomes a migration project. Developers have been burned by that already. They don't want their product roadmap to be hostage to a single vendor's release schedule or pricing decisions.

The second is that no single model is actually the best at everything. When you look at a real product, it's not one call, it's a workflow. You might have a classification step, a retrieval step, a generation step, a summarization step. The quality, latency, and cost profile you want for each of those is different. A small, fast model might be perfect for routing or extraction, and you only want to pay for a big frontier model on the one step that really needs the reasoning. Being model agnostic lets you compose that instead of overpaying everywhere.

The third piece is control and risk. A lot of the teams we talk to are thinking about data privacy, about where their traffic goes, about what happens if a provider deprecates a model or changes behavior under them. Open models and a model-agnostic architecture give them an escape hatch. Even if they're using a closed model today, they want to know they can swap it out without rewriting the application.

And honestly, I think there's a mindset shift happening. Early on, people treated the model as the product. Now the mature teams treat the model as a component, like a database or a compute layer. You evaluate it, you benchmark it, you pick the right one for the job, and you expect to change it over time. Once you think about it that way, being model agnostic isn't a nice-to-have, it's just good engineering. The hard part is making that swap genuinely easy, because in practice the prompts, the tool calling formats, the fine-tunes, all of that leaks into your application. So the infrastructure layer has to absorb a lot of that complexity so developers don't have to.

r001.rationale: It says the model landscape changes almost weekly and that hard-wiring a product to one model turns each shift into a migration project, motivating developers to avoid dependence on a single model.

astra-6.text:
I think developers want the freedom to choose the best model for their application, and that choice can change very quickly. One model might give you better quality for a particular task, while another gives you lower latency or a better cost. Even within one product, you may want different models for different parts of the workflow.

If you tightly couple your application to a single model, every time something better comes along, you have to do a lot of work to adopt it. Developers want to focus on their product and their users, while retaining the flexibility to evaluate models and switch when it makes sense. The models aren’t interchangeable—you still have to test their behavior—but your infrastructure shouldn’t be the thing that prevents you from making that choice.

r001.rationale: The response says model choices can change quickly and that new, better models motivate developers to avoid tightly coupling their products to one model.

sol-6.1.text:
Developers want the flexibility to choose the best model for their application. Different models have different strengths, and you’re always balancing quality, latency, and cost. You might use a more capable model for a difficult reasoning task and a smaller, faster model for something simpler.

And the models are evolving so quickly. If a better model comes out tomorrow, you want to be able to take advantage of it without rebuilding your whole application. So being model agnostic gives developers room to experiment, compare results on their own workloads, and change as their needs change.

r001.rationale: The response says models are evolving quickly and developers should be able to adopt a better model without rebuilding the application, clearly explaining why they avoid tying products to one model.
